forms.translit: la ba'i na bza' can gyi zhabs

proposals.definition: Kambalāmbarapāda, the siddha to whom the manuscript attributes song 8; the name means 'he whose garment is a blanket'. In the refrain and couplet 3 he calls himself Kāmali, an Old Bengali form of kambala, 'blanket'. Munidatta calls him a siddha master (cp.08.m2). The Tibetan has la ba'i na bza' can, 'wearer of a woollen garment', and la ba pa.
proposals.rationale: The poet of song 8, already named p-kambala in the unit; keep-source with -pāda as for the other siddhas, with Kambala and Kāmali (his self-naming in the song) as variants.

proposals.definition: Devakrī, the name of the rāga (melodic mode) to which song 8 is sung, given in its heading. The Tibetan translation calls the melody lha rnams rol pa, 'play of the gods', as if the name were Sanskrit devakrīḍā, 'divine play'; whether krī is a shortened form of that word is uncertain.
proposals.rationale: The glossary has no entry for this rāga; like the other rāga names it stays in source form in the heading.

proposals.definition: Gold (Old Bengali sonā). In the first line of song 8 the boat of compassion is filled with gold, leaving no place for silver; the Tibetan translation has gser. Munidatta's paraphrase has the boat filled with the essence of the true guru's grace, through identity with emptiness endowed with all supreme aspects (cp.08.m2).
proposals.symbolicImage: the gold with which the boat of compassion is filled

symbolicReadings.referent: the essence (rasa) of the true guru's grace, with which the boat, bodhicitta, is filled through its identity with emptiness endowed with all supreme aspects (his paraphrase puts this where the song has 'filled with gold'; he gives no explicit gloss of the gold)

proposals.rationale: Gold and silver are the opening images of song 8 and Munidatta's comment turns on them; 'gold' is the plain rendering, confirmed by the Tibetan gser.

proposals.definition: Silver (Old Bengali rūpā, Sanskrit rūpya). In song 8 the boat is so full of gold that there is no place to put silver; the Tibetan translation has dngul. Munidatta takes rūpā as rūpa, 'form', the first of the aggregates, which have no separate place (cp.08.m2); the Tibetan commentary keeps the sound, rU pa.
proposals.symbolicImage: silver, for which there is no place in the boat full of gold

symbolicReadings.referent: form (rūpa) and the other aggregates, feeling, perception, formations and consciousness, which have no separate place, since everything is made of that (a play on rūpā, 'silver', and rūpa, 'form')

proposals.rationale: The word invites the rendering 'form' because of Munidatta's pun, so an entry fixes 'silver' in the line and sends the aggregates to a note.

proposals.definition: A stake or post (Old Bengali khuṇṭi), apparently the one the boat is moored to: in song 8 it is pulled up before the boat sets off. Munidatta writes khuṇṭikā; the Tibetan translation has brtod phur, 'tethering stake', in the song and the comment. Munidatta reads it as the fault of appearance (cp.08.m3).
proposals.symbolicImage: the stake pulled up before the boat sets off

symbolicReadings.referent: the fault of appearance (ābhāsadoṣa), which the best of yogis is to pull up once he has made the guru's word firm; the Tibetan commentary has the guru's word producing firmness against the fault of appearance, without the pulling up

proposals.rationale: A boat image with an explicit gloss in the commentary; 'stake' is the plain sense of khuṇṭi and matches the Tibetan brtod phur.

proposals.definition: A rope, apparently the boat's mooring line (Old Bengali kācchi; Munidatta has kacchikā; the Tibetan translation nyag thag, 'rope'). In song 8 it is let loose once the stake is pulled up. Munidatta's gloss speaks of loosening a thread of knowledge (vidyāsūtra); the Tibetan commentary has the thread of ignorance (cp.08.m3).
proposals.symbolicImage: the rope let loose once the stake is pulled up

symbolicReadings.referent: a thread of knowledge (vidyāsūtra), to be loosened so that the boat runs swiftly; the Sanskrit reads kacchikāsu vidyāsūtrañ ca, and the Tibetan commentary has instead 'the rope is the thread of ignorance' (ma rig pa'i srad bu), as if reading avidyāsūtra

proposals.rationale: The second piece of boat gear in couplet 3, with a gloss on which the Sanskrit and the Tibetan disagree; 'rope' follows the Tibetan nyag thag and the context of casting off.

proposals.definition: A word of uncertain sense in song 8: in 4a the rower climbs onto the māṅga and looks in four directions; 5a has māgā. Munidatta renders both as mārga, 'path'; the Tibetan translation takes them as the boat's stern (gru yi mjug) and prow (gru sna). The source form is kept for now.
proposals.symbolicImage: the māṅga the rower climbs onto before looking in four directions

symbolicReadings.referent: the path (mārga) that is the joy of cessation (viramānanda): one who, lacking the guru's lineage, goes on it and looks in the four directions at the grasped and the rest falls into saṃsāra
for māgā in 5a: the path, the joy of cessation, to which bodhicitta has gone, purified by one's own knowledge, once left and right have entered the middle channel

proposals.rationale: The two witnesses disagree on what the word is (a path or a part of the boat), so the source form is kept and glossed until the reviewer chooses.

proposals.definition: A companion, or company (Old Bengali saṅga; the edition prints sa(su)ṅgā, marking a doubtful vowel). In the last line of song 8 the rower meets great bliss on the road as companion; the Tibetan translation has grogs, 'companion'. Munidatta speaks of obtaining the embrace of Nairātmā-knowledge, the companion of great bliss (cp.08.m5).
proposals.symbolicImage: the companion met on the road with great bliss

symbolicReadings.referent: the knowledge of Nairātmā (nairātmājñāna), the companion of great bliss, whose embrace the poet says he has obtained on that path; the Tibetan has 'the knowledge of selflessness'

proposals.rationale: The song ends on this image and Munidatta names what it stands for, so an entry keeps 'companion' in the line and Nairātmā in the note.

proposals.definition: Utprekṣā, 'poetic fancy': in Sanskrit poetics, a figure of speech (alaṅkāra) that imagines one thing as if it were another. Munidatta says calling bodhicitta 'boat' in song 8 is such a figure (cp.08.m2), as he does for the body-tree of song 1. The Tibetan here has gzugs kyi rgyan, perhaps for rūpaka, 'metaphor'.
proposals.rationale: A term of poetics that Munidatta uses to say how the images are to be read; the reader of the woven commentary needs it explained.

proposals.en: emptiness endowed with all supreme aspects

forms.translit: rnam pa thams cad dang ldan pa'i stong pa nyid
forms.lemma: rnam pa thams cad dang ldan pa'i stong pa nyid

proposals.definition: Emptiness endowed with all supreme aspects (sarvākāravaropetā śūnyatā): emptiness understood not as a bare absence but as bearing every excellent quality, a phrase of Mahāyāna and especially Kālacakra literature. Munidatta says the boat, bodhicitta, is filled, through identity with this emptiness, with the essence of the true guru's grace (cp.08.m2).
proposals.rationale: A fixed doctrinal phrase, distinct from plain emptiness (sunyata), that a reader of the commentary would need explained; the English follows the usual sense of the compound.

forms.translit: rab tu mi gnas pa gsal bar mdzad pa
forms.lemma: rab tu mi gnas pa gsal bar mdzad pa

proposals.definition: A work Munidatta cites as the Apratiṣṭhānaprakāśa ('Illumination of the Non-abiding'; Shastri restores the syllable pra); it is not otherwise identified here. He quotes its verse: every concept arising in the mind is to be given up; blissful joy and dispassion alike are mere conception; nirvāṇa is nothing other than the mind free of concepts (cp.08.m2).
proposals.rationale: A work quoted by name in the commentary; titles stay in source form, and the Tibetan title confirms the restored reading.

proposals.definition: An oar, or perhaps a steering paddle. In song 8 the rower asks how he can row with no oar; the manuscript spells the word keṛuyāla there, and the Tibetan translation has gru skya, 'boat oar'.
proposals.rationale: New form for the existing entry: the spelling with ya (keṛuyāla) in cp.08.4b, which the existing form keṛuāla does not match, and the Tibetan gru skya read off that line.

proposals.definition: Left and right. In song 8 the rower presses left and right (bāma dāhiṇa); the Tibetan translation has byang dang lho, 'north and south', which its commentary explains as left and right. Munidatta reads them as the two appearances made to enter the middle channel (cp.08.m5).
proposals.rationale: New forms for the existing entry: the reversed order bāma dāhiṇa (the existing form is dāhiṇa bāma), Munidatta's pratīka, and the Tibetan 'north and south' (form only, not a match, since it would claim every 'north and south').

proposals.definition: A road or way (Old Bengali bāṭa). In the last line of song 8 great bliss is met on the road (bāṭata, locative); the Tibetan translation has lam du. Munidatta says 'on that path' (tasmin mārge) (cp.08.m5).
proposals.rationale: New form for the existing entry: the locative bāṭata of cp.08.5b.

proposals.definition: Nirvāṇa. In the verse of the Apratiṣṭhānaprakāśa that Munidatta quotes in song 8, nirvāṇa is nothing other than the mind free of concepts (cp.08.m2); the Tibetan renders it with the verb mya ngan 'da' ba, 'pass beyond sorrow'.
proposals.rationale: New forms for the existing entry: the accusative nirvvāṇaṃ (existing forms are nirvvāṇañca, nibāṇe, nivvāṇe) and the Tibetan verbal rendering.

proposals.definition: A river boat. Song 8 opens with the boat of compassion (karuṇā nābī) filled with gold. Munidatta says bodhicitta is called the boat, as a poetic figure (cp.08.m2), and quotes Śāntideva on the boat of a human birth, hard to find again.
proposals.rationale: New forms for the existing entry: nābī in the song and Munidatta's nāvīti, and the boat (nāvam, nauḥ) of the Bodhicaryāvatāra verse he quotes. The bare nābī has no safe literal match (see questions).

proposals.definition: A practitioner of yoga. In song 8 Munidatta addresses the practitioner as yogivara, 'O best of yogis' (cp.08.m3); the Tibetan has kye'i mchog gi rnal 'byor pa.
proposals.rationale: New form for the existing entry: the vocative compound yogivara, which none of the existing forms covers.

proposals.definition: The wheel of great bliss. In song 8 Munidatta twice joins it with an ocean (samudra), the goal toward which the boat is rowed (cp.08.m2, cp.08.m5); the Tibetan has bde ba chen po'i 'khor lo.
proposals.rationale: New forms for the existing entry: two compounds in cp.08.m2 and m5; the stem মহাসুখচক্র as a match covers them and any inflection.

proposals.definition: Appearance. In song 8 Munidatta reads the mooring stake as the fault of appearance (spelled ābhāṣa) and speaks of the two appearances, left and right, made to enter the middle channel (cp.08.m3, cp.08.m5); the Tibetan has snang ba.
proposals.rationale: New forms for the existing entry: the spelling ābhāṣa with ṣ in cp.08.m3 and ābhāsadvaya joined by sandhi in cp.08.m5, where it opens with the vowel sign rather than the letter আ.

questions: Match forms: the proposal schema has no matchRe field, so where a bare Old Bengali word could hit inside other words I used a longer literal: বাহতু কামলি for p-kambala (a bare কামলি could sit inside, say, kāmalipta), সোনে ভরিতী for gold (a bare সোনে could be so'ne- written without avagraha), রূপা থোই for silver (a bare রূপা sits inside rūpādi and svarūpa), and মিলি মাগা for manga (a bare মাগা may be the verb 'ask'). I left the boat's new form নাবী (cp.08.1a) unmatched: a bare নাবী hits inside compounds such as vāsanābīja, and করুণা নাবী would swallow the karuna hit, because the longest form wins. If you want whole-word regexes in matchRe instead: (?<![\p{L}\p{M}])কামলি(?![\p{L}\p{M}]), and the same pattern for নাবী, সোনে, রূপা and মাগা.

māṅga (4a) and māgā (5a): Munidatta renders both as mārga, 'path' (cp.08.m4, cp.08.m5); the Tibetan translation makes them the stern (gru yi mjug) and the prow (gru sna) of the boat. I proposed keep-source-first-gloss. If you want an English rendering, 'path' follows Munidatta, but 'climbing onto the path' fits 4a less well than a part of the boat does.

kācchi / kacchikā (cp.08.m3): Munidatta's 'kacchikāsu vidyāsūtrañ ca' (a thread of knowledge) against the Tibetan 'the rope is the thread of ignorance' (ma rig pa'i srad bu) may point to a lost a- (avidyāsūtra), which deserves a witness note. The manimula entry records kacchikā again in cp.14.m4. I did not add a bare কচ্ছিকা match, so that occurrence stays unlinked until you decide whether it is the same word.

ubesem̐ (cp.08.2a): I did not add it to upadesa. Munidatta's paraphrase has uddeśena, 'toward' (cp.08.m2, cp.08.m5), and the Tibetan has 'looking at the sky' (nam mkha' bltas nas), so it may be uddeśa rather than upadeśa. The same paraphrase puts 'the ocean of going to the wheel of great bliss' where the refrain has the sky. The gagana entry lists its reading as unattested, and a merge cannot add readings to an existing entry, so you may want to add cp.08.m2 to gagana by hand. The same goes for boat: in cp.08.m2 bodhicitta is called the boat, and karuṇā is named as twilight language.
kala: if its match includes the bare কাল, it will hit kālo in the Bodhicaryāvatāra verse of cp.08.m2, where kāla is 'time' (it is no time for sleep), not Death.

Witness points for the drafter: the Tibetan of couplet 3 (cp.08.3b) has no name where the Bengali names Kāmali. In cp.08.m4 the Tibetan credits the quoted line 'fallen in a ditch, camphor perishes' (Sanskrit caryāpādaḥ) to Kṛṣṇācārya's song, which the Sanskrit does not; I added nothing to p-kanha for it.

companion: saṅgā may not be a noun at all. In cp.13.5b the same phrase has mahāsuha sāṅge ('with great bliss'), which the Tibetan also renders as bde ba chen po'i grogs. If saṅgā here is the postposition 'with', the entry can go, and Munidatta's reading can move to a note on the line. The Tibetan grogs is a form only, not a match, because as a match it would also catch 'O friend' (kye'i grogs) in cp.17. Munidatta's mahāsukhasaṅga (cp.08.m5) has no match either: any literal long enough to be safe would contain মহাসুখ or নৈরাত্মা and suppress those hits.

Matches checked across the text so far: no hits inside unrelated words turned up. Two things the check surfaced: cp.13.m3 quotes the same Apratiṣṭhānaprakāśa verse and introduces it with nāgārjunapādāḥ, so you may want to credit the work to Nāgārjuna in its entry. And cp.13.5a has suṇata māṅge, apparently the same māṅga, which my match (মাঙ্গত) does not catch; cp.14.4b has bāma dāhiṇa dui māga, 'left and right, two paths', which supports Munidatta's 'path' for māgā.
